utterances.text: So you didn't do -- your answer is you didn't do any paperwork after you made that agreement not to be commander anymore?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, the administration saw to the paperwork. The administrative services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you came in on the 15th to the command, did you ever -- did you become commander at that point, before you went to Zvornik, or were you still a guy that had been no longer commander and on annual leave?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. But I think there was some paper that I signed. I think it was a report of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Not as commander. I signed it because I think it was a three-monthly report about the work of the detachment. And as I was commander during a certain period of time, I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you just told us you didn't do any paperwork, that the paperwork was done by administrators. So are you now telling us that you did do some paperwork?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He said do paperwork. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if he wants to coach the witness, I think we can do it outside the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, at this point I see no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I see a big problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's continue the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to this misleading -- he said he didn't do paperwork. If we could have a clarification, doing -- physically doing, because we're talking about a cultural divide here, versus signing paperwork. If he could clarify it, I don't have a problem. But there's a big difference between who physically does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure the cultural divides can be worked out on redirect, but this is just pure obstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you had told us that you hadn't done any paperwork initially. Everyone heard that. And now on the 15th, you're telling us you may have signed some documents, such as some sort of annual report.

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: It's like this: The administration had prepared the report beforehand. Now, as at that time, the late Oficir was in Sarajevo with his unit. It should have been sent out much earlier. And I was on annual leave. I wasn't there. So Oficir couldn't have signed it. And then this report, which referred to the 4th, 5th, and 6th, or rather April, May, and June, those months, and when it came, they said it had to be sent out, so I signed it so that it could be sent out. So that was purely based on what had gone beforehand, what had happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you testified in this courtroom that you had no authority as commander after your deal in June. Now you're telling us that you signed an official report as commander on 15 July. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: It's like this: I signed, but everything that was stated in the report -- I always had to send out monthly reports for April, May. I don't know whether a report was sent out for June. These were regular reports. So I signed the previous reports. So it was a conglomeration of the reports I had sent out previously, my monthly reports set out in a three-monthly report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you signed it as commander on 15 July. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, I signed it. Now, whether I signed it as the commander, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you did sign it as a commander on 15 July, or any time in July, that would have been wrong, according to your testimony, and you wouldn't have done that, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: No. I'm telling you I signed the report, the report on the work of the detachment for April, May, and June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So on 15 July at least, you were authorised as commander to sign reports?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, it was just a report which I had sent out to the brigade individually, these reports. And then the report was to have been sent out on the 5th. And as the late Oficir was in the field all the time, he didn't sign it or send it. So when I turned up, I just signed it so that they could dispatch the report off as soon as possible. I didn't think it was any important bit of business, that I wasn't violating anything of that kind. Because it was all sent out, the contents of that report were the contents of the monthly reports that had been sent out previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this a police report done in time of war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Well, it was a report about the work of the detachment. I don't know whether it was a police one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The detachment report in time of war. It's a pretty darn important report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And command is a pretty darn important position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: I'm saying again that the report had already been sent out individually for every month. So this was the sum total of the three monthly reports that had already been sent out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And command is a very important position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There are grave responsibilities a commander has in the detachment. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the -- your detachment had a Praga. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a -- what looks like an anti-aircraft weapon mounted on the back of a special flatbed truck?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your attachment had what's called a BOV?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a similar vehicle to a Praga but instead, it's one big armoured unit with similar sorts of weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: A BOV, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had a tank as well, I take it, a T-55?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever -- did that tank and its crew, were they ever on standby in Bratunac in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may object here, I don't think there's anything in the indictment charging Mr. Blagojevic with June 1995. So I just want to point that out for the record because I'm being told we should focus on the indictment itself. So the critical period is after, so if there's something now I have to defend in June 1995, I surely would like to know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe this question goes to the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a tank and/or its crew on standby in Bratunac in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about the Praga? Was it ever -- in 1995 ever on standby or in ready in Bratunac, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't remember where your platoon of heavy equipment was located?

utterances.speaker: MILOS STUPAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I've got an exhibit that has been marked as P853. Defence has had this for several years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point in time, I just want to point out that when they were cross-examining, we were being given exhibit lists at the beginning of the day. It appears now we're not only getting them not before the day, but we're getting them in the middle of cross-examination. And I want to point out on the record the very severe language of the Appeals Chamber with respect to the Krstic trial. Because Mr. McCloskey was a member of that trial team when there was some significant hiding of the evidence for the Defence. So I do take exception to this. We have the evidence. We don't have equality of arms. We've got millions of documents. At least we should have the courtesy of having an exhibit list and may I note I requested an exhibit list prior or during the break, and I was told we would be -- that they needed to consult with Mr. McCloskey. There was a consultation, but we received nothing. And so I do take exception to these cat and mouse techniques.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the allegations continue fast and furious in front of witnesses. Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas was provided a collection of special police documents in October of 2002. They were searchable, and they were provided to him and his Defence team. And if he would put his witnesses lists on there, he would have come up with various documents. And I mean, I don't want to put his case together for him. But there is no Rule 68 in this exhibit. I did not provide it to Mr. Karnavas before today here, but I provided it to him years ago. He is a fine lawyer. He has the ability to search his own record. I do not believe that there's any rule or any practice that requires me to give material that is clear and is obvious over to the Defence again and stack it up to them. Your Honour, if there is such a rule, I will follow it. But there's not such a rule that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not asking for that, Your Honour. I'm asking for common courtesy. This document, the exhibit list was prepared yesterday, last night at 7.00. It's common courtesy. We showed up every day and every morning. Right before the session we provided an exhibit list so they could go ahead and search their documents anticipating what we would do on cross-examination. I'm not suggesting that they point out where the exculpatory material is. But I think it's common courtesy to do this. And might I again remind everybody what the Appeals Chamber said in Krstic, and I don't want to be in a position on appeal making the same argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, at the very beginning of the trial, we made a ruling on this aspect. We said that before the cross-examination, the party conducting the cross-examination should furnish at least a list of the documents they are going to use during the cross-examination, which will greatly facilitate the proceedings of the present case. I hope, Mr. McCloskey, you could do that for your next witness before you take the stand to cross-examine that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Furthermore, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We also believe, Mr. Karnavas, you only have five minutes left, we believe that during the night, I mean tonight, you could search your documents and be prepared for tomorrow's cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour. We did. That's why I know the document exists. I'm now given a translation. Obviously, they took the time of translating this. We were never provided with a translation. What I am trying to demonstrate here is the gamemanship that's going on. We searched our documents. We located -- which is in the local language. Now, we're being given documents that they have translated. Obviously, they have an obligation to give us those translated versions. At least we could check the translations against the original. That's what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you should have raised this issue long before, ever since you got those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are millions of documents that are not translated. What I am suggesting is once they translate documents, there is a continuing obligation for them to provide those translated documents to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's absolutely absurd, Your Honour. He is making up law as he goes. We have to now translate all the documents to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not saying this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is insanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If they translate it, they should give it to us, that's all I'm saying, especially if they are going to use it. That's all I'm saying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In that respect, I agree with you. If this document is going to be used in these proceedings, they have to be translated and it has to be furnished to the other party and to the Bench before doing the cross-examination. Well, Mr. McCloskey, I think it's almost time. It seems to me that you could not finish the cross-examination for today. Could we break now, and we'll resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. The hearing is adjourned for today. And Witness, I'm afraid that we have to keep you here for another day because the proceeding has not finished yet. Originally, we hoped we could send you back today, but it seems to me that it's impossible. So you have to be back tomorrow morning to continue the proceedings. And during the period that you are staying in The Hague, please do not talk to anybody or please do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I give every witness this kind of warning. This is not for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
